title: Elephants in gold
hook: drunken elephants decked in gold, horses swift as deer, kings in glory, and all leave this world empty-handed (Savaiye 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ascetics, and your line, nothing without love. This week you closed the Jaap: courage borrowed, more names than stars, all the names, japji then jaap. Then the savaiye opened: by your grace, and nothing without love. Today, the second verse. Day three hundred sixty-four.

The parade comes down the road and the crowd goes quiet. First the elephants, huge and swaying, drunk on their own strength, hung with gold so that they flash in the sun. Then the horses, thousands of them, quick as deer, barely touching the ground. Then the kings, broad in the shoulder, and on either side of them, rows and rows of people bowing their heads. It's the most powerful thing anyone in the crowd has ever seen. And then the poet leans over and whispers one question. Today: elephants in gold.
screen: `ELEPHANTS FLASHING WITH GOLD.` → `HORSES QUICK AS DEER.` → `KINGS, AND ROWS OF BOWED HEADS.`

segments.voice: That's the second savaiya. In paraphrase: maddened elephants decked in gold, tall and matchless. Horses by the million, faster than deer. Mighty kings before whom countless heads bow. Then the question: and what of it? Such great kings there have been, and at the end they went away barefoot. Barefoot. That's the picture the verse uses. In the Guru's world, a king never walked anywhere. He rode. So the one who arrived on an elephant leaves on his own bare feet, carrying nothing. Empty-handed, the way everyone leaves. Here's what keeps this from being easy moralizing. Guru Gobind Singh knew this world from the inside. He held court at Anandpur. He rode fine horses, and Sikh tradition tells of an elephant called Prasadi, brought to the young Guru as a gift. He wasn't a poor man shaking his fist at the palace. He was someone who'd seen the gold up close and knew what it could and couldn't do. Notice too what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say elephants are evil, or that horses are sinful, or that owning beautiful things is wrong. Sikhs aren't asked to give up their homes or their work. The savaiya simply follows the parade to its end, past the gates of the city, to the last walk every king takes. And on that walk the gold stays behind. In the full line, the reason is named too: these kings did not remember the Lord. What's left after the gold, the verse suggests, is the only thing that was worth carrying.
screen: `ELEPHANTS, HORSES, BOWING HEADS.` · `AT THE END, THEY LEFT BAREFOOT.` · `THE GURU KNEW THE GOLD UP CLOSE.` · `NOT A BAN ON BEAUTIFUL THINGS.` · then, large: `THEY LEFT EMPTY-HANDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one thing you own and smile. Pick it up if you can: a watch, a mug, your phone, a ring. Hold it and really look at it. Where it came from, what it's been through with you. Breathe slowly. Now let yourself enjoy it, honestly, without guilt. Then let a second thought sit beside the first: one day it won't be yours. Not as a sad thought. As a light one. Smile at it the way you'd smile at a friend you know you'll part from one day. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you set it down. The bell holds the time.
Elephants in gold. The second savaiya's parade of power: elephants, horses and bowing heads, and kings who still left this world barefoot.
Your line: they left empty-handed. Today, when you catch yourself wanting something shiny, picture the barefoot king, and see if the wanting gets a little lighter. Day three hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this as the second of the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning; it is often explained as a reminder that wealth and power stay behind when a person dies.

fork.setup: the great kings ride past on elephants hung with gold, and countless heads bow. the poet asks: and what of it? how does the verse answer?
options: at the end, they went away barefoot.
fork.reveal: in the full verse, such kings did not remember the Lord, and at the end they left barefoot. a king never walked; now he walks out with nothing.

original.note: Gurmukhi: maate matang, maddened elephants, the opening words of the second savaiya.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse telling people that wealth is bad.
what it means: a parade of power followed to its end: the kings who rode in leave barefoot, and the gold stays behind.
what a scholar hears: matang is an old Sanskrit word for elephant, and the verse's last image is the king going on his own bare feet, a pointed reversal in a world where kings rode.

sources.work: Sikh historical tradition (e.g., Bhai Santokh Singh, Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth)
